concept to provide in situ particle size information for several smoke aerosols (solid and liquid). The 
enhancements will be made by using commercial diagnostic techniques to provide droplet size 
information. Due to space, crew time and mass limitations, the measurements will be aggregate 
moments of the aerosol size distribution. By combining three such moments, it is possible to calculate 
the particle arithmetic mean diameter, the diameter of average mass and, by assuming a log-normal 
particle distribution, the geometric mean diameter and standard deviation. The experimental design and 
practical application of the data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code to predict the

actical application of the data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code to predict the 
smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the 
pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. 
The results of the experiment will include statistics of the smoke particle size distribution for several 
practical spacecraft materials for a range of smoke generation conditions and measurement of a readily 
modeled reference material for validation of smoke growth models. The work fits directly into critical 
needs of the future manned exploration missions by providing the data needed for the design and 
implementation of spacecraft smoke sensors for future manned missions.

Summary and Conclusions: 
This study examined the characteristics of eight types of wire: anodized mild steel, pure 
iron, Alomega (similar to Alumel), -Stainless steel, pure platinum, platinum-rhodium, 
tungster-5%rhenium, and tungsten-26%rhenium. Traditional heating wires, Nichrome 
and Kanthal were also included for comparison. 

Pure platinum has close-to-ideal characteristics. However the cost of the material may be 
prohibitive. 

Alomega and stainless steel ran a close second. 

Mild steel, iron and tungsten-composites oxidized in the oven and their characteristics 
changed significantly from one thermal cycle to the next. 

Nichrome and Kanthal have too flat a slope to meet the objectives.

INTRODUCTION 
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument is an experiment payload planned for 
the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS). Throughout 
this document the term “project” is used to refer to the SAME project in its role as payload developer. 
1.1 
Purpose 
The purpose of this Software Description Document is three-fold: 
(1) to describe the Software Management Plan (SMP) for the project 
(2) to identify what product specification and procedure documentation will be produced as part of the 
software effort for the project, and 
(3) to identify and describe the records that will be produced as part of the software effort.

Introduction and background 
In the earliest missions (Mercury, Gemini and Apollo), the crew quarters were so cramped that it was 
considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, 
included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors (Friedman, 1992). These devices were limited to 
line-of sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The Space Shuttle was developed 
in a time (1970’s) of rapid progress in smoke detection for terrestrial applications (Bukowski and

(scattering or obscuration detectors) were generally unavailable due to the difficulty of producing stable 
light sources. There was no data available concerning the smoke particle size distribution in low-
gravity and the database of normal-gravity smoke characteristics was a fraction of what is available 
today. There was also no data on spacecraft dust particle size distributions but the absence of 
gravitational settling suggested that there would be more large particles than are seen on earth. 
Consequently it is understandable that the Orbiter design employed a variant of the accepted ground 
based approach (ionization detectors). The Orbiter has

1.1 Scientific background 
1.1.1 
Spacecraft fire detection 
In 1996 the Comparative Soot Diagnostics Experiment (CSD) flew in the Orbiter Middeck as a 
Glovebox payload (Urban, 1997, A & B). The CSD experiment was designed to produce small 
quantities of smoke from several sources and determine the response of the ISS and Orbiter smoke 
detectors to these sources. In addition, a goal was to obtain particulate samples from these sources. As 
will be described below, the experiment operated very effectively and marked differences in the 
performance of the detectors compared to their behavior in 1-g were observed. In extreme cases, the 
detector used in the Orbiter was completely blind to easily visible smoke from sources that were readily 
detected in 1-g. It

. In extreme cases, the 
detector used in the Orbiter was completely blind to easily visible smoke from sources that were readily 
detected in 1-g. It is hypothesized but as yet unverified that this performance difference was due to 
enhanced growth of liquid smoke droplets in low-g. 
As described by Friedman (1994) there have been six overheat and failed component failures in the 
NASA Orbiter fleet (Space Transportation System or STS). None of these events spread into a real fire 
but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997

improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is critically needed. As will be shown below, the 
CSD results clearly demonstrate that solid-particulate smoke-aerosols in low-g have larger average 
dimensions than those produced in 1-g and that spacecraft smoke detector design cannot be based on 
1-g understanding and experience. Consequently a more complete data base of likely spacecraft 
smoke particulate is needed, particularly in the pre-fire pyrolysis period. The CSD experiment provided 
significant data on solid particle smoke sources but due to limitations in the design did not produce 
particle sizes for liquid aerosol smokes. Liquid smoke ae

t data on solid particle smoke sources but due to limitations in the design did not produce 
particle sizes for liquid aerosol smokes. Liquid smoke aerosols are produced by many pyrolyzing 
flammable materials and the smoke droplets can be expected to coalesce on contact, producing 
spherical particles, with significantly different properties from the aggregate structures produced by 
solid particulate. The objective of the SAME experiment is to bring improved diagnostic technology to 
the measurement of smoke particulate for various practical materials to allow more effective 
characterization of the particle size distribution. A modeling program will be developed to examine the 
parameters that control the growth of these smoke droplets between the source and the sensor. These 
results a

parameters that control the growth of these smoke droplets between the source and the sensor. These 
results are critically needed to allow design of reliable smoke detection systems for long duration low-

Prior to CSD, no combustion-generated particulate samples had been collected near the flame zone

therefore only corresponded to the early stages of a fire or were collected far from the flame zone. The

gravity may be significantly larger than those in normal gravity (1-g). This raises new scientific 
questions about soot processes as well as practical issues for particulate size sensitivity and detec-

An excellent review of fire detection technology at the approximate time the Space shuttle was under

(pyrolyzing) materials produce larger particulate, owing to the large amount of condensed, unoxidized

(ELF) experiment objective was to study fundamental phenomena related to the mechanisms 
controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. The design modifications made as

1.3 EXPERIMENT OVERVIEW 

The predecessor investigation to Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) was called 
Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) and was developed by NASA/GRC for flight on the Shuttle 
Spacelab during the Fourth United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-4 / STS-87) mission in 
November 1997. 

SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena related to understanding the mechanisms 
controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. SPICE will stabilize an enclosed 
laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and numerical 
predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to verify 
flame structure predictions.

Executive Summary
This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke
aerosol relative to smoke on Earth.
We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with
the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the
International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about ﬂuid/thermal/particle
interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is
expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain,
convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric con-
ﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophor

wnstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric con-
ﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity,
buoyancy produces asymmetries in all ﬁelds of interest and ampliﬁes vapor-to-particle conversion near
room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling re-
moves large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼40 µm and the mode
particle size to ∼5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmet-
ric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity
when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large

particle mode does not appear in microgravity ﬂows that do not have prominent high temperature re-
circulation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle

Introduction
Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convec-
tion modiﬁes the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles,
condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the
aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles
with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high
temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems
(Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than
those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al.,

al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than
those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity
smoke particles to be 2 −8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover,
large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles
with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al.,
1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than ﬁve times greater in microgravity (Liu
et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design
of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, inc

ffects is of practical interest because it assists in the design
of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the Interna-
tional Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may
not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al.,
2005).
The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the inﬂuence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke
growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate
(DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation
via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated

to identify the ﬂuid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two cross-

4.1
FLOW CONFIGURATION
We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air ﬂowing over a heated sample that expels
DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conﬂagration stage of a ﬁre studied in experi-
ments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is
shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and ﬂows over a heated rectangular sam-
ple. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected
downstream for analysis. The ﬂow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation
to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,

ABSTRACT
The primary scientific explorations of this thesis work are to better understand (a) 
microgravity fire-suppression of untested extinguisher, (b) combustion kinetic model 
refinement of renewable fuel butanol (C4H9OH) isomers, and (c) directly induced cool 
flame dynamics of higher n-alkane fuels from an isolated small droplet combustion 
perspective employing computational fluid dynamics with comprehensive chemical 
kinetics. The chronological development of the research direction shifts from a relatively 
small fuel like methanol (CH3OH) to heavier straight paraffinic fuel n-decane (n-C10H22). 
The first installment of the thesis is directed towards answering the feasibility of then-
newly considered fire suppressant xenon (Xe) for microgravity space application by the 
Nati

The second installment of the thesis outlines the efforts directed towards 
improving the gas phase kinetic model of butanol isomers based on droplet combustion 
experiments and computations. This is a unique contribution where the traditional gas-
phase experiment/theory-driven kinetic model is further refined in light of critical 
recommendations from the droplet combustion analysis. The comprehensive kinetic 
model of Sarathy et al. (Combust. Flame, 2012) is one of the two widely used model for 
butanol isomers which has been extensively validated against homogeneous gas phase 
experiments. The numerical simulation of the butanol droplet combustion experiments at 
atmospheric conditions predicted the faster burning rate and larger flame diameter using 
the above model. An exhaustiv

the above model. An exhaustive perturbation analysis is carried on chemical,

synthesized results from this huge variable-matric perturbation revealed that the isomer-

1. Overview 
The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 

The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire 
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard 
L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and 
the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). 

Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is

ngton University of St. Louis and 
the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). 

Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. 
Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. 
For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha 
Nayagam who are also with CWRU. 

The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing.

2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a 
solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes 
Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. 

Overview: 
Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing 
research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. 
Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This 
could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. 

It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by

mpeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. 

It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed 
with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad 
range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool 
diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. 

Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be 
required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the 
Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight 
experiment.

The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests 
with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that 
accurately models these conditions. 

Intellectual Merit: 
Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame 
chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool 
flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose 
understanding has large economic consequences.
